messages.subject: Accessing values from HBase using Column Name
messages.subject_clean: Accessing values from HBase using Column Name
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was trying to read from HBase.
I have a table in HBase where I only have one ColumnFamily.
In that ColumnFamily I am storing two Columns. While retrieving the value from HBase I was trying to access the columns by Column Name. If I use indexed approach it retrieves fine. But while trying to retrieve by Column Name I could not find any way to do so. Please help.

Here is what I was trying.

=======================================
hb.new.table("data", "base");
hb.insert("data",list( list(1,c("base:Name", "base:Value"), list("name1", "value1"))))
rows<-hb.scan("data",start=1,colspec=c("base"))
readval <- rows$get()

for ( i in 1:length(readval) ) {
    # this is to print the Name and corresponding value
    print("Name = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][[1]]);
    print("Value = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][[2]]);
}
=======================================

When I do the above it prints the Name and Value just fine.
[1] "Name = "
[1] "name1"
[1] "Value = "
[1] "value1"

*************************************************************
But what I was trying to do is to access the HBase output by Column Name.
I need this because I might have different no of Columns of each row and depending on the name of the Column the order gets changed.

Let me insert another row in the same table.
Here I will store 3 columns in the columnfamily named "base".

=======================================
hb.insert("data",list( list(2,c("base:Name", "base:Value", "base:Desc"), list("name1", "value1", "This is a description"))))
=======================================

Now the above code will not print the correct Name and Value.

What I was trying to have is somewhat to access like this. ( The below code doesn't work, I have mentioned just to give a feel )

=======================================
for ( i in 1:length(readval) ) {
    # this is to print the Name and corresponding value
    print("Name = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][["base:Name"]]);
    print("Value = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][["base:Value"]]);
}

# OR May be like this

for ( i in 1:length(readval) ) {
    # this is to print the Name and corresponding value
    print("Name = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][["Name"]]);
    print("Value = ")
    print(readval[[i]][[3]][["Value"]]);
}
=======================================

Thanking you.

Regards,
Souvik.

messages.subject_clean: Problem in reading files stored in HDFS
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am confused about accessing files stored in HDFS (uploaded by some other program e.g. Hadoop command line utility) from R using rmr packages.
I am trying to explain with an example.
Say I have two csv files (For simplicity I have taken csv files more complex for binary files)
One is a.csv and other is b.csv
Initially both are residing in local filesystem.
I'll upload these files in HDFS one through R and one through command line.
Once those are stored in HDFS I would like to read the content of the files from R.
Here goes the first case.

===========================================
to.dfs("a.csv", output="/user/hduser/a.csv")
read.csv(values(from.dfs("/user/hduser/a.csv"))[1][[1]]) # reads the csv file correctly
===========================================

Now let me upload the b.csv from command line.

===========================================
$ /usr/local/hadoop/bin/hadoop dfs -copyFromLocal b.csv /user/hduser/b.csv
===========================================

Now if I try to read the file from R like

===========================================
read.csv(values(from.dfs("/user/hduser/b.csv"))[1][[1]]) # failed to read the file
===========================================

It fails to read the files.
Rather it reads the several key, value pairs (Keys I can not correlate, It is an non-sequential increasing series and Values are lines of the CSV file.
Note: For binary files it seems a chunk of the file is returned for each key

I understand that the way R puts the file in HDFS and the command line does are different and hence the issue.
But there must be an mechanism from R to read the files stored in HDFS by non-R programs (Like command line).

I tried to use hdfs://master_node_ip_address:50075/user/hduser/b.csv but it fails.

In Java you can do like this Path pt=new Path("hdfs://ip_address:port/user/hduser/b.csv")
I am not a Java expert but this probably works (I googled and found such things).

Now I clearly understands the in Java there are surely libraries which know how to interpret hdfs://path_to_files.

In R how to do it?

Now why do I need this. Say these filenames are stored in HBase and I want to read each file within Mapreduce program.

Please do advise and feel free to get back to me in case of any question.

Thanks and regards,
Souvik.

Hi,
 the fact that you talk about from.dfs and send an example without any call to from.dfs is certainly not helpful. The parallelism level depends on your hadoop configuration, at least for the map phase, so you may want to test it with some java code, like the built in examples, to be sure you can leverage your cluster in full and take rmr out of the equation for a moment. Your data set is not that big so it is likely that hadoop doesn't think worth it to unleash more than one process at it. See below an example of reading 1M records in 2 seconds, that is not what hadoop was invented for. from.dfs doesn't aim for parallelism, its role is to load into main memory the results of a computation when they are of a reasonable size (small GBs) so that's not the point. The call that triggers mapreduce jobs which should be parallel is mapreduce, but there you don't specify the vectorized option so it's reading a line at a time  which should be about 1K times slower than vectorized =T. It's a problem with the csv parser, you won't see this kind of speed ups using vectorized in other contexts, but it really is mandatory when reading csvs. This is for 1M records

on a meager mac laptop. Keep also in mind that if you specify the format wrong read.table can take forever, just forgetting the headers can be a big deal. Try to read.table(.. ) in the first 1M records and see how it works. from.dfs calls read.table behind the curtains for the csv format.
Finally, there is one thing that you need to do to be able to handle big data. You need to start on small data sets (in local mode) and then build up to the real thing. We have a nifty debugging guide document up on the wiki in need of some company. At each level, new bugs and problems pop up and they get harder to troubleshoot, so you are much better off making sure that your code works for 10, 100, 1000 etc records before you unleash it on 35M, it doesn't work, game over. It's not only rmr that needs to be developed for like that, this is a generally accepted reality of developing for big data that I just learned from others  and from experience and pass it on to rmr users.

Greetings,

Two questions:

1) My impression of the examples was that the user reduce(k,vv) was called once per a key?

2) Suppose that the map associates so many values to one key that in the reduce it is impossible to load them all into memory at once in the Reduce. Java gets around this with an iterable interface on values in the org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.Reducer.reduce(key,values,context). How is it handled in RHadoop?

Thanks,
Jeremiah

I think the issue is more about flexibility in handling different use cases.  Those of us whose IT infrastructure employs Microsoft's Active Directory for user groups and permissioning is, I believe, just another use case, if you will.  Microsoft (in their infinite wisdom :-] ) does things like put spaces in their groups - for the default group is "domain users".

That said, RMR parses plain text into a data structure using white space as a delimiter (in this case of hadoop operations like -ls, there are probably others), instead of using another method, such as an api call to get explicitly defined data structure of, in this case, the parameters of a filesystem listing.  I posit that RMR could parse this structure more intelligently to handle this use case, perhaps through use of a regular expression.  I am not familiar enough with the source code to implement the change myself.
File: master/rmr/pkg/R/mapreduce.R
Line: 319
Function: hdfs.match.out

x <- "drwxr-xr-x   - mfuery domain users           2 2012-07-31 19:06 /user/mfuery/output.tsv"
m <- regexec("([drwx-]+)[ ]+(.)[ ]+([a-z].*?)[ ]+([a-z].*?)[ ]+([0-9]+)[ ]+([0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}) ([0-9:]+)[ ]+(.*)", x)
data <- regmatches(x, m)
data
[[1]]
[1] "drwxr-xr-x   - mfuery domain users           2048 2012-07-31 19:06 /user/mfuery/output.tsv"
[2] "drwxr-xr-x"

[8] "19:06"

This does not eliminate the ambiguity of user+groups, but I don't really see the use of this information from within R.  You'd have to make some system calls to parse /etc/passwd or whatever, then match against that data structure, but I don't see the point.

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#254] reduce(k,vv) what if vv is to large to fit in memory?
messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#254] reduce(k,vv) what if vv is to large to fit in memory?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Aug 21, 2012 at 10:18 AM, jeremiah rounds <roundsj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Greetings,
>
>
> Two questions:
>
> 1) My impression of the examples was that the user reduce(k,vv) was called once per a key?

Correct

> 2) Suppose that the map associates so many values to one key that in the reduce it is impossible to load them all into memory at once in the Reduce. Java gets around this with an iterable interface on values in the org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.Reducer.reduce(key,values,context). How is it handled in RHadoop?

It is not. You need to use a larger key space or a combiner, that is avoid the problem with algorithm changes. While there is an iterator library in R the concept is not in very widespread use. This simplified or R-idomatic or whatever you want to call it reduce interface has been extremely well received by users and having control on the number of shuffle keys and distribution of data over those keys is any way good mapreduce programming practice (if I have one reducer take all the work, it doesn't help that it doesn't run out of memory if it doesn't terminate in a reasonable amount of time). I understand that it is a trade off and I haven't proven that one can always solve memory issues in the reduce phase by using a combiner or maybe an expanded key range and an additional job or in-memory post processing, but the experience so far has been generally positive and using combiners has other performance advantages and should be encouraged. It seems to me, again without any proof, that the only advantage of iterating through the values associated with a key in the reducer could be that one can apply more classical streaming algorithms (streaming not in the hadoop sense, in the theory of algorithms sense, that is when memory <<  input size) reading one value at a time. When using  a combiner, one has to work on whatever group of values is available on the map side, which can be large or small, create a summary or intermediate state of some sort and then combine those states on the reduce side. It is a more "lumpy" model of computation (see this <http://www.cs.utah.edu/~jeffp/papers/merge-summ.pdf> for example) but I think it is very effective in mapreduce and  in many ways an emerging model. If you add to this that R performs best when using vectorized primitives and that it is a lot more complex, at least for the average R user, to write a stateful reducer, which is necessary with multiple reduce calls per key, the choice seemed pretty clear. I'd be happy to hear of use cases that support or negate this design choice and we may revisit it in the future, for instance providing an iterator interface. Thanks

Antonio

David
